questions.topic: Definition, need and applications of machine learning
questions.text: What is machine learning? Give two real-world applications.
questions.ideal_answer: Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence in which computers learn patterns from data and improve their performance on a task with experience, without being explicitly programmed with rules. A model is trained on examples and then used to make predictions or decisions on new data. Applications include email spam filtering, product recommendations on e-commerce sites, fraud detection in banking, and speech recognition in voice assistants.

questions.text: What are the main types of machine learning?
questions.ideal_answer: Supervised learning trains on labelled data, where each input has a known output, and is used for classification and regression. Unsupervised learning works on unlabelled data and finds hidden structure, such as clustering and dimensionality reduction. Semi-supervised learning uses a small amount of labelled data with a large amount of unlabelled data. Reinforcement learning trains an agent to take actions in an environment to maximise cumulative reward through trial and error.

questions.text: What is the difference between multi-class and multi-label classification?
questions.ideal_answer: In multi-class classification, each example belongs to exactly one class out of three or more classes, for example classifying a fruit as apple, banana or mango. In multi-label classification, each example can belong to several classes at the same time, for example a movie tagged as both comedy and romance. Binary classification is the special case with only two classes. Multi-class models often use softmax output, while multi-label models usually use a separate sigmoid output for each label.

questions.text: What is the difference between linear regression and logistic regression?
questions.ideal_answer: Linear regression predicts a continuous numeric value, such as a house price, by fitting a straight line y = mx + c, and is usually trained by minimising mean squared error. Logistic regression is used for classification: it passes a linear combination of features through the sigmoid function to output a probability between 0 and 1. A threshold, usually 0.5, converts the probability into a class. Logistic regression is trained by minimising log loss, also called cross-entropy.

questions.text: How does the K-Nearest Neighbour algorithm classify a new data point?
questions.ideal_answer: KNN stores all training examples and does no explicit training, so it is called a lazy learner. To classify a new point, it computes the distance, usually Euclidean, from the new point to every training point. It selects the K closest points and assigns the class that is most common among them, by majority vote. K is usually chosen as an odd number to avoid ties, and features should be scaled because distance is sensitive to their ranges.

questions.topic: Naive Bayes classifier and Bayes' theorem
questions.text: How does a Naive Bayes classifier decide whether an email is spam?
questions.ideal_answer: Naive Bayes uses Bayes' theorem: the posterior probability of a class given the features is proportional to the prior probability of the class times the likelihood of the features given the class. It assumes the features, here the words in the email, are conditionally independent given the class, which is the naive assumption. So it multiplies the prior probability of spam with the probability of each word appearing in spam emails, and does the same for not spam. The class with the higher posterior probability is chosen. Laplace smoothing is used so that unseen words do not make a probability zero.

questions.text: A model has 99 percent training accuracy but 70 percent test accuracy. What is the problem, and why does it happen?
questions.ideal_answer: This is overfitting, which means the model has high variance. It has memorised the training data, including noise, instead of learning general patterns, so it does not generalise to new data. It usually happens when the model is too complex for the amount of data, such as a very deep decision tree. Remedies include getting more data, simplifying the model, regularisation, pruning, using cross-validation and early stopping. In contrast, low accuracy on both training and test data would indicate underfitting or high bias.

questions.topic: Decision trees: ID3, entropy, information gain, Gini
questions.text: Why does a decision tree choose the attribute with the highest information gain for a split?
questions.ideal_answer: Entropy measures the impurity or uncertainty of a set of examples; it is zero when all examples belong to one class and highest when classes are evenly mixed. Information gain is the entropy of the parent node minus the weighted average entropy of the child nodes after the split. The attribute with the highest information gain reduces uncertainty the most, producing the purest child nodes. This gives a smaller tree that classifies faster and generalises better. CART uses Gini impurity for the same purpose.

questions.topic: Confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC
questions.text: A fraud detection model shows 99 percent accuracy, but only 1 percent of transactions are fraud. Why is accuracy misleading, and which metrics would you use?
questions.ideal_answer: With such imbalanced data, a model that predicts not fraud for every transaction already gets 99 percent accuracy while catching zero frauds. So accuracy hides poor performance on the minority class. I would use the confusion matrix and focus on recall, which is the fraction of actual frauds detected, and precision, which is the fraction of flagged transactions that are actually fraud. The F1 score balances both, and precision-recall AUC is more informative than ROC-AUC for heavy imbalance. The decision threshold can then be tuned based on the cost of missed fraud versus false alarms.

questions.text: K-means gives different clusters each time you run it on the same data. Why, and how would you choose K and get stable results?
questions.ideal_answer: K-means starts with randomly chosen initial centroids and converges to a local minimum of the within-cluster sum of squares, so different initialisations can lead to different clusters. Using k-means++ initialisation spreads out the starting centroids and gives better, more consistent results. Running the algorithm several times, using the n_init parameter, and keeping the solution with the lowest inertia also helps, and a fixed random seed makes it reproducible. K can be chosen using the elbow method on the inertia plot or the silhouette score. Features should be scaled first, since K-means uses distances.

questions.text: Your team has a dataset with 500 features and only 2000 rows, and the KNN model performs poorly. How would you explain the problem and what would you do?
questions.ideal_answer: This is the curse of dimensionality: as the number of features grows, data points become very sparse and distances between points become nearly equal, so nearest neighbours are no longer meaningful. With few rows and many features, the model also overfits easily. I would first remove irrelevant or redundant features with feature selection. Then I would apply PCA after standardising the data, which projects the data onto a few principal components that capture most of the variance, choosing the number of components by explained variance such as 95 percent. I would then retrain and compare using cross-validation, or try a model less sensitive to dimensionality.

questions.topic: Support vector machines and kernel functions
questions.text: You need to classify data that cannot be separated by a straight line, and you are considering an SVM. How would you set it up and tune it?
questions.ideal_answer: An SVM finds the hyperplane that separates classes with the maximum margin, defined by the support vectors. For non-linearly separable data, the kernel trick maps data into a higher-dimensional space where a linear separator exists, without computing that space explicitly; the RBF kernel is a common choice, and polynomial kernels are another option. The C parameter controls the trade-off between a wide margin and misclassification, with large C risking overfitting, and gamma controls how far each point's influence reaches in the RBF kernel. I would scale features, then tune C and gamma using grid search with cross-validation. For very large datasets, SVMs can be slow, so a linear SVM or another model may be preferred.
